strengths: The problem is well motivated and practically relevant: making small grounding VLMs competitive with much larger ones at lower deployment cost is a worthwhile and timely goal.

The empirical results are broad and consistent: EGM is applied to six checkpoints across two families (InternVL-3 and Qwen3-VL) and improves vanilla and amodal grounding in almost all cases, which is a non-trivial amount of evidence for the general applicability of the recipe.

The proposed amodal grounding setting (predict the full extent of an occluded referred object) is a reasonable and underexplored task for VLM-based referring, and the curation pipeline with a GPT-4 verification filter (App. B, Fig. 7-9) is a sensible first-pass construction.
The paper documents implementation details (SFT/RL hyperparameters, rollout settings, prompt templates, dataset sizes), which makes re-implementation of the two-stage SFT+GRPO recipe plausible.
Qualitative examples (Fig. 10-11) are informative and illustrate the intended behavior (key-feature-focused reasoning) versus the verbose reasoning of the 235B thinking model.
weaknesses: The central framing is not supported by the experiments. The title and abstract advertise "scaling test-time inference" / "#generated tokens" as the mechanism, but the gains come from supervised fine-tuning on GPT-4-generated reasoning traces plus GRPO reinforcement learning, i.e. a training-time recipe. No controlled test-time scaling (budget forcing, self-consistency, best-of-N, extra sampling at inference) is performed, and EGM is never compared against simply spending more inference compute on the untrained model; hence the headline claim about test-time scaling is not demonstrated.

The technical method has little novelty relative to the existing literature: answer-conditioned GPT-4 reasoning distillation plus GRPO is exactly the R1-style recipe (Guo et al. [15], Shao et al. [33], and the learnability-based data selection of Evans et al. [14]) transplanted to grounding. Prior reasoning/RL-for-grounding work (e.g. VLM-R1, Visual-RFT, Vision-R1, Seg-Zero and related GRPO-for-perception papers) is neither cited nor used as a baseline, so the paper's incremental position is unclear.

The diagnostic that motivates the paper (Sec. 3, Table 1, Fig. 2) is not adequately validated. Failure categories ("COMPLEX_PROMPT" 62.8%) are produced by asking GPT-4 to label failures, with no human verification, no agreement statistics, no confidence calibration, and an unstated subset size; the claim that small VLMs fail because of text understanding rather than visual handling is inferred from "visual encoders are similar" rather than tested with a controlled experiment (e.g., giving the small model a disambiguated description, or holding visual ability fixed).

Table 1 actively contradicts the paper's scaling narrative and is left uncommented: Gemini-2.5-Pro (22.1%) and Gemini-2.5-Flash (20.9%) are worse on the same COMPLEX_PROMPT failures than InternVL-3-32B (29.9%) and InternVL-3-78B (42.6%). If a frontier model underperforms a 32B open model by 20 points on this subset, the subset is more plausibly dominated by dataset/prompt-format artifacts than by "size"; the authors never discuss this, even though it undermines the stated rationale.

The same anomaly affects Table 3, raising questions about the evaluation protocol: GPT-5 averages 42.6 and Gemini-2.5-Pro 63.8 RefCOCO/+/g accuracy while Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct reaches 84.2. A single prompt template derived from the InternVL/Qwen formats (Fig. 5) applied to API models is very likely to break their output parsing, and in Table 3 the InternVL baseline numbers are taken from official reports (marked *) while all EGM numbers are self-measured, mixing measurement sources within the same comparison. The reported conclusion of EGM superiority, especially margins of ~1 point, is therefore not trustworthy as-is.

There are no ablations whatsoever. SFT-only vs. RL-only vs. SFT+RL, reasoning-trace quality/faithfulness, the learnability-based data selection (vs. random/uniform selection), the reward weighting alpha, and the effect of reasoning length are all untested, so no component of the method can be attributed with the observed gains.

The amodal benchmark and metric do not establish that the task is non-trivially solved. The evaluation set is constructed by the same proprietary VLM pipeline used to build the training data (text prompts generated and self-verified by GPT-4, ~50% filtered), the only metric is a 0.5-IoU success rate on amodal boxes, and there is no baseline showing that simply predicting the visible (modal) box cannot already pass this criterion, nor any comparison to classical amodal detection on COCO-Amodal/TAO-Amodal. The "we are the first to study amodal grounding in VLMs" claim is asserted rather than substantiated against prior amodal/VLM work.

The headline quantitative claim is fragile: "EGM-Qwen3-VL-8B achieves 91.4 IoU vs. Qwen3-VL-235B's 90.5" rests on a 0.9-point difference on a thresholded accuracy metric with no error bars, no multiple seeds, and no significance testing, and the abstract mislabels this accuracy (fraction of samples with IoU>0.5) as "IoU". A ~1-point margin over a model 30x larger should not be presented as outperforming it without variance estimates.

The efficiency argument is incompletely evidenced. Only EGM-vs-235B latency is reported; there is no comparison of EGM latency/token count against the vanilla small model it replaces, which is the relevant cost of the added reasoning, nor any accounting for the substantial one-off cost of generating 575K GPT-4 reasoning traces and running GRPO. The "GPU latency in practice = latency x number of GPUs" metric is unconventional and favors multi-GPU baselines without justification.

Distillation data has a potential answer-leakage problem: reasoning traces are generated by a teacher that is shown the ground-truth box (Fig. 6, "The image shows a green bounding box indicating the Ground Truth target object"), so the traces are rationalizations of a known answer rather than reasoning toward it. The paper does not analyze whether the student learns generalizable localization reasoning or dataset-specific cues, and the marginal gains for some models (e.g. InternVL-3-8B, +1.1 avg) are consistent with the latter.

Reproducibility is limited: the promised code/website are placeholders ("coming soon" on the first page), and core steps (reasoning generation, amodal prompt generation, failure categorization) depend on a proprietary VLM, so no part of the pipeline as described can be fully reproduced from the submission.

The manuscript is visibly unfinished: leftover placeholder links, duplicated/empty table cells and typos in tabular material ("INTernVL", "GGemini"), incomplete reference entries (e.g. [2] "Qwen3-vl, 2025" with no venue/link), and over-claimed statements in the introduction and conclusion.
